fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Every poison is a cure at the right dose", "body": "Chance Garton opens Taurus season with the plants that folklore both prizes and fears. His guests are Fiona Heckels and Kaz Goodweather, the Seed Sistas out of the UK, whose book Poison Prescriptions centers on the nightshade family, on datura, belladonna and henbane. Their argument is that poison and potion share a root, and that a poison is simply a curative agent whose whole character is decided by dose. These plants still sit inside allopathic medicine for asthma and Parkinson's, which makes them, as the Sistas put it, the bridge between magic and medicine."}, {"title": "Escaping the green allopathy trap", "body": "Both guests trained in phytotherapy at a medicalized London course, in an old Victorian hospital with bars on the treatment room windows and a rule about how many colors you could wear in your hair. They describe being taught plants through projectors and lists of chemical compounds while never going outside. Chance names the same problem from his conversations with Kyle Denton on astro herbalism, a green allopathy that trains herbalists to repress symptoms exactly as pharmaceuticals do. The Sistas answer with valerian, chili and daisy blended into a passion potion, built to open circulation and expression rather than sedate it."}, {"title": "Plants as characters you can actually meet", "body": "The heart of the Seed Sistas method is reviving folklore by giving each plant a personality and then performing it. Rosa canina becomes Rosa Hearts Petal, a grandmother midwife who holds you and then slaps you out of self indulgence, and her overlooked hedgerow sister the bramble keeps her door open with berries and tea. Apple carries the Latin name malus domestica, domesticated evil, and sulks about being blamed for Eden. Chance links this to Althea, Artemis and Achilles living inside marshmallow, mugwort and yarrow, and calls it a revival of the bardic tradition."}, {"title": "Magic on the hoof and the emergent tradition", "body": "Asked how magic enters beyond chemistry, the Sistas answer that it comes down to vibes, tuning forks, the pulse of the earth, and speaking or singing aloud so the plant feels the resonance of a human voice. A friend once called their approach an emergent tradition, and they had previously called it magic on the hoof. Out in the hills you rarely have the purple candle a book prescribes, so the work becomes reciprocity, asking what the space and the plant need. Chance reflects that flowing with source feels like making it up, and that making it up is what makes it authentic."}, {"title": "Certificates, shame and the words we are not allowed to say", "body": "The pair admit a paradox. They find certification abhorrent yet print certificates with daisies and hawthorn because people want them, and they carry insurance because events demand it. Their real teaching is discernment, that if you cannot comfortably ask a question you are in the wrong room. That same refusal of shame runs into the flying ointment, the solanaceae preparation behind the witches on broomsticks story, and into sacred sexuality and the word cunt, which they trace through Uma Dinsmore and her book Yoni Shakti. Chance offers Kunti from the Mahabharata as another possible root."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Fiona Heckles and Kazz Goodweather are better known in the UK as the Seed Sistas, and this dynamic duo has been energetically encouraging initiation in the herbal arts for over 20 years. Tune in to learn about expressing instead of repressing, valerian potions, make-your-own folk mythos, the character of rose, brambles and hedgerows, earth magic, and the vibe of creativity.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the 2nd hour, we go in-depth on their latest book, Poison Prescriptions, exploring the history of poisons & poisoners, anesthetics and the mystery of consciousness, datura, henbane, and crossing the river Styx, the beer purity laws forbidding herbal brews, raving with Belladonna and Dionysus, Mugwort, the witches flying ointment, and malevolent magics.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Poisoning as a Profession", "body": "The second hour opens on history rather than pharmacology. Chance points out that the French poisoner Catherine Monvoisin carried poison inside her own name, and adds that the famed Phoenician royal purple came from the murex, a dye that was itself lethal, so poisoning and royalty ran together for a very long time. The Seed Sistas trace poisoners retained by Caesars and courts to remove inconvenient people, the enslaved Haitians who won their freedom partly through herbal knowledge and poisoned water sources, and monkshood carried as an arrow tip poison into early warfare."}, {"title": "Insight Inside the Delirium", "body": "The Seed Sistas describe belladonna's strange run through nineteenth century medicine, when it was given for alcoholism and other addictions in American hospitals and the man who founded Alcoholics Anonymous reported meeting the divine under its influence. They point to hospital notes recording people who surfaced from atropine carrying answers they had no background to reach, including a businessman whose commercial tangle untied itself while he was under. Their reading is that medicine has largely looked past all of this, because the same compounds bring delirium and the line between delirium and genuine insight is narrow."}, {"title": "The Law That Erased a Brewing Tradition", "body": "Henbane carries a jovial, expansive reputation, and the Seed Sistas connect it to Jupiter rather than to the Saturn of its relatives, and to Pilsen in Bohemia, where whole villages grew the herb because it was the brewing plant of choice and lent its name to the beer. The Munich beer purity law of 1500, which they call the very first drug law ever passed, swapped it for hops. Chance reads that as the monastic system doing what it always did, and as a false binary between Protestant and Catholic masking the same interests behind both wings."}, {"title": "Three Plants, Three Personalities", "body": "Working with blindfolded groups over many years, the Seed Sistas say each of the three plants carries a distinct character they can watch play out afterwards. Henbane reads as the most expansive and uplifting, and strangers in the room end up talking easily to one another. Datura sends people almost immediately inward, and they tie it to werewolf lore, to visions of human figures covered in fur, and to shape shifting, which they read as counsel on moving between the roles society asks of us. Belladonna is the forceful one, embodying Atropos, the fate who cuts the thread of life."}, {"title": "Hexing the Idea, Not the Man", "body": "Asked about the people who turn up wanting help cursing someone, the Seed Sistas say they would rather leave others responsible for their own ill intent, since they feel deep rage themselves but refuse to carry and amplify somebody else's hatred. What they do hex is the capitalist system and consumerism, invoking Atropos to cut its threads, a spell they say runs underneath Poison Prescriptions. They also reject the tidy split between white and black magic, and describe turning five hundred years of pressure on the medicine woman into satirical theater and creative activism instead of cursing."}]
